mutant.description: Outcome.forStatus's first range takes 200 too (status <= 200), so WebMvcTags.outcome labels a 200 response INFORMATIONAL instead of SUCCESS. It breaks preservation at status 200 and only there; the label stays in the finite set, so the finite-outcome property holds on the mutant by design.

notes: Concrete controls only: each revision's slice (WebMvcTags, and after's Outcome, compiled from the commit by JDK 8 with the recorded flags against Framework 5.2.0.RC2, micrometer-core 1.2.0 and javax.servlet-api 4.0.1) in its own JVM, on JDK 21 and 25, over the probes null; 99, 100, 199, 200, 299, 300, 399, 400, 499, 500, 599, 600; Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE. Observed: tag key and value, normal or exceptional termination and the exception's class. Object identity is excluded on purpose: the patch moves the tags' allocation and caching from WebMvcTags to Outcome. Scope: an extracted source slice, not the commits' own builds.

The slice's check against Spring's own build (the user's decision of 2026-11-14): the after slice and Boot 2.2.0.M6's published spring-boot-actuator JAR, which carries after's two source files, each with the slice's dependency JARs, in its own JVM on JDK 21 and 25, with replay's driver, probes and oracle. Expected: the same observations and the same oracle problems on each JDK. It checks that the slice behaves like the published build of the same sources; it is no evidence about before, which has no published counterpart.

For a null response or a response whose getStatus() returns any int, both revisions give the same tag key and value and the same specified exceptions. No allowed-change region: the change is meant to preserve every input. The old path's HttpStatus.Series.resolve divides by 100 (truncating towards zero), so it agrees with Outcome.forStatus's ranges on every int, negative ones included: that is the hypothesis this task tests, not a result.

The family's bounded-label property, as an absolute property of one revision: every result has key 'outcome' and a value among INFORMATIONAL, SUCCESS, REDIRECTION, CLIENT_ERROR, SERVER_ERROR and UNKNOWN. Established would say this one tag dimension is finite on this entry, not that the server or the release is secure.
The same property and domain as finite-outcome-before, on after's artifact: one property, two claim identities.

The mutation control's concrete side: after and the constructed mutant (after's sources with controls/status-200.patch applied, built by after's recipe), each in its own JVM on JDK 21 and 25, with replay's driver, probes and oracle. Expected: after holds, and the mutant fails at status 200 and only there.

The mutation control: preservation's claim, its file and domain unchanged, over the mutation pair, after against the constructed mutant. Expected refuted, at status 200 and only there. Sensitivity evidence for the preservation claim, never a historical result.

blockers.summary: Predicted from the build files, not from a build: at both commits Boot is 2.2.0.BUILD-SNAPSHOT, and spring-boot-dependencies pins 14 pre-release versions, among them SNAPSHOTs (Spring Data Moore-BUILD-SNAPSHOT, Spring Security, AMQP, Batch, Integration and Kafka BUILD-SNAPSHOTs) and milestones from https://repo.spring.io/milestone (Spring Framework 5.2.0.RC2, Reactor Dysprosium-RC1). A SNAPSHOT is a mutable reference whose 2019 contents are gone (repo.spring.io/snapshot keeps only each SNAPSHOT's last builds), so the exact-commit Maven build cannot be reproduced, even with decision 1's extension to repo.spring.io. The user's decision (2026-11-14): the narrower source-slice route instead, each commit's WebMvcTags (and after's Outcome) compiled by JDK 8 against Framework 5.2.0.RC2's spring-web, spring-webmvc and spring-core (with spring-jcl), micrometer-core 1.2.0 and javax.servlet-api 4.0.1, labelled extracted-source-slice in every receipt. Checked by hand (a note): with -g -parameters -source 1.8 -target 1.8, the after slice's WebMvcTags.class and Outcome.class are byte-identical to Boot 2.2.0.M6's published ones (sources.lock.json); the m6-replay task replays M6's JAR beside the slice. The blocker stays for the exact commits' builds, which no task here claims.

Predicted from a static scan, not from an attempt, for all three native tasks (preservation, finite-outcome-before, finite-outcome-after): jvmcontract gaps on WebMvcTags.outcome reaches java.util.regex.Pattern.compile in WebMvcTags.<clinit> and java.util.Objects.requireNonNull in micrometer's ImmutableTag.<init>, on both sides, each with no approximation, so refused by name under gaps strict. Neither is in the changed code. Run by hand with a binary one lib/src commit old, on JARs that are not the commits' builds (records/outcome-gaps.json, a note). Class initialization is never removed to get past it.

Predicted from lib/README.md: the parameter is javax.servlet's HttpServletResponse, a library interface, and the checker dispatches invokeinterface only to application methods and passes an interface-typed dependency null (refused if reached). The claims' domain is a null response or one whose getStatus() returns any int (claims/outcome-preservation.json); an attempt that can only take the null response is that refusal, and the claim stays unresolved, never re-read as the null-only domain. The finite-outcome property also reads the result through micrometer's Tag interface (getKey, getValue). The replay's carrier covers the int domain concretely.
